Who I am

I'm a physics and physical science teacher candidate at San Diego State University, completing my Single Subject Preliminary Teaching Credential alongside a B.A. in Physical Science. I've spent over 600 hours planning and teaching science in real classrooms — 8th grade science and high school physics — and I can't imagine doing anything else.

My approach centers on inquiry, hands-on exploration, and building the kind of genuine relationships with students that make learning feel meaningful. I'm also currently serving as the 2025–2026 California Student Liaison to the Commission on Teacher Credentialing, where I represent preservice teachers from SDSU and advocate for credential candidates statewide in Sacramento.

At the core

I believe science is best learned by doing — by wondering, investigating, and making sense of real phenomena through evidence. Every student deserves access to rigorous, engaging science in a classroom built on trust and high expectations.

Teaching philosophy

My concept of learning

Learning, to me, is a process of building understanding — not simply receiving information. In science, mastery means a student can take an observation from the real world, connect it to a mechanism, and use evidence to defend an explanation. A successful learning situation is one where students are confused in a productive way: asking questions, revising ideas, and growing more precise in how they think and communicate. I know learning has happened when a student can apply a concept to a new phenomenon — not just recall it for a test.

"When one of my 8th graders revised her underwater color model after our diffraction grating lab — not because I told her to, but because her data disagreed with her prediction — that was the moment I knew she understood what science actually is."

My concept of teaching

I aspire to be a teacher who opens doors. My core belief is that every student is capable of engaging meaningfully with rigorous science — and that my job is to design the conditions that make that possible. I value transformational learning: the kind that changes how a student sees the world, not just what they know. A perfect teaching situation is one where students are doing the intellectual work — arguing over evidence, revising their models, explaining ideas to each other — while I circulate, listen, and prompt rather than tell.

My goals for students

Beyond content knowledge, I want students to leave my class with three durable skills: the ability to construct an evidence-based argument, the habit of questioning their own assumptions, and the confidence to say "I don't know — let's find out." I also prepare students to write and speak scientifically, because communicating your reasoning is as important as the reasoning itself.

My teaching methods

I anchor my units in real phenomena — things students can see, touch, or genuinely wonder about. My five-lesson Light Waves segment began with a single question: why do colors disappear underwater? From there, students investigated wavelength with diffraction gratings, ran depth simulations, analyzed close-reading visuals, and ultimately wrote CER paragraphs defending a scientific explanation. I use inquiry-based learning, think-pair-share, structured investigations, and science modeling regularly, and build in differentiated supports so language barriers or learning differences don't prevent access to the science.

My interactions with students

The relationship comes first. I learned every student's name within my first week of student teaching and made it my business to know their interests, their struggles, and what made them tick. I'm especially committed to students who have historically struggled with school or science: I've built relationships with high-need and behaviorally challenged students by offering consistency, clear expectations, and genuine care. An observer in my classroom would see me crouching next to desks, asking "what do you notice?" rather than "did you get it right?"

Assessing learning

I use formative assessment continuously — circulating during activities, scanning written work mid-lesson, calling on students to explain their reasoning. Summatively, I favor performance tasks: model revisions, CER paragraphs, lab reports. I use criterion-referenced grading and prioritize giving students meaningful feedback over marking answers right or wrong.

Professional growth

I treat my own development the way I ask students to treat theirs: with honesty, humility, and a genuine appetite for improvement. I reflect after every lesson, actively seek feedback, and regularly arrived early during my credential program to share ideas and solicit critique. Serving as the California Student Liaison to the CTC has pushed me to think about teaching as a profession with obligations to the broader community of educators. I intend to pursue my M.A. in Mathematics and Science Education and remain a learner for as long as I teach.

Engage & explore — light color mixing

56 min · Developing & Using Models · MS-PS4-2

Central focus: Students investigate how light behaves and how different wavelengths relate to color. They observe a light color-mixing activity, take notes on wavelength and white light, and develop an initial model predicting which colors will disappear first at depth — then propose a testable investigation plan.

Key learning: Distinguish observation language from prediction language; identify a variable to change and an outcome to observe; produce Model 1 using RGB, wavelength, and white light concepts.

RGB light mixingModel 1 predictionSentence framesIEP/504 supportsThink-pair-share
📄 Lesson 1 — Full edTPA lesson plan

Investigate — diffraction grating & ocean depth simulation

56 min · Planning & Carrying Out Investigations · MS-PS4-2

Central focus: Students measure the wavelength of red, green, and blue light using a diffraction grating, then complete an ocean-depth simulation using blue gel filters to observe how color visibility changes with depth.

Key learning: Record observation-based data; use absorb/transmit vocabulary to revise Model 2; write an evidence phrase linking absorption to wavelength in water as a medium.

Diffraction gratingAbsorb / TransmitDepth simulationModel 2 revisionPartner rehearsal
📄 Lesson 2 — Full edTPA lesson plan

Analyze — close reading & crabs/plankton evidence task

45 min · Developing & Using Models · Patterns · MS-PS4-2

Central focus: Students analyze a close-reading visual to identify which colors are absorbed first in water, explain investigation guidelines for producing reliable evidence, and begin the structured Crabs & Plankton evidence task.

Key learning: Cite specific visual evidence; distinguish wavelength-specific absorption from uniform darkening; write claim-evidence statements using cause/effect connectors.

Visual analysisRefractionInvestigation guidelinesClaim-evidence writingFunds of knowledge
📄 Lesson 3 — Full edTPA lesson plan

Investigate — full crabs & plankton lab

56 min · Planning & Carrying Out Investigations · MS-PS4-2

Central focus: Students carry out the full Crab and Plankton Lab with consistent procedures, collecting evidence across multiple evidence cards, identifying patterns in color visibility at increasing simulated depths, and producing a written evidence-based pattern statement.

Key learning: Follow investigation guidelines with fidelity; record observations across depth zones; write a connection statement linking depth, absorption, and animal color perception.

Crab & Plankton LabData recordingPattern statementsGroup collaboration504 accommodations
📄 Lesson 4 — Full edTPA lesson plan

Synthesize — final model revision & CER paragraph

45 min · Developing & Using Models · Patterns · MS-PS4-2

Central focus: Students synthesize evidence from the full learning segment to write a CER paragraph explaining why colors disappear underwater, and produce a final model revision showing absorption and transmission of different wavelengths in water.

Key learning: Select and justify evidence; use absorb, transmit, wavelength, and medium in cause/effect reasoning; write a CER with at least four evidence references and a clear claim.
